name: Tigris
license: Proprietary (SDKs and CLI MIT; TigrisFS and the TAG cache Apache 2.0)
summary: Globally distributed S3-compatible object storage that moves data to where it’s read, with no egress fees.
intro: Tigris answers the S3 API at one endpoint, `https://t3.storage.dev`, with the region set to `auto`. Stateless API gateways in each region take requests close to the client. Object metadata (where each object lives, user metadata, permissions) is kept in FoundationDB, a transactional key-value store, replicated between several clusters; object bytes go to block stores in the region nearest the writer. In the default Global bucket, metadata is pushed to every region and data is pulled on demand: the first read from another region makes a local copy there, and over time data settles where it is read most. Reads in the same region are strongly consistent; reads from other regions may briefly return an older version. Single-region, Dual-region and Multi-region buckets pin data instead. Buckets can also be snapshotted and forked without copying data. There are 8 regions: San Jose, Chicago, Ashburn, Amsterdam, Frankfurt, London, Singapore and Tokyo.

Standard storage costs $0.02 per GB-month, Infrequent Access $0.01 and the two archive tiers $0.004. Writes cost $0.005 per 1,000 and reads $0.0005 per 1,000, and nothing is charged per GB out, from any region. The price is the same for every location type, with no charge for replication. Infrequent Access has a 30-day minimum and a $0.01 per GB retrieval fee; the archive tiers have a 90-day minimum. Each month 5 GB, 10,000 writes and 100,000 reads are free. Tigris started on Fly.io, where `fly storage create` makes a bucket and sets the `AWS_*` secrets on an app. The service itself is closed source; its SDKs, CLI, the TigrisFS FUSE file system and the TAG caching gateway are open source.
strengths: One endpoint and no egress fees: data written in one region is served locally in others without setting up a CDN or replication
Strong consistency within a region, conditional writes, and whole-bucket snapshots and zero-copy forks
Wide S3 coverage, including object tagging and ACLs; S3 storage class names map to its tiers
Built into Fly.io’s CLI, and runs on Tigris’s own hardware rather than on a big cloud
limits: Standard storage at $0.02 per GB-month costs more than R2 and nearly as much as S3 Standard, and two and a half to three times Wasabi or B2 per TB; reads and writes are billed per request
Global buckets are only eventually consistent across regions, and a GET or HEAD for a key that doesn’t exist checks other regions, which can add several hundred milliseconds
The default Global bucket keeps a single copy placed by access pattern; for data that must ride out a regional outage, Tigris recommends Multi-region
Eight regions, a closed-source service and a young company (paid since July 2024)
Infrequent Access and archive tiers bring minimum durations (30 and 90 days) and retrieval fees

sections.title: Next to S3 and R2
sections.intro: Wasabi, Backblaze B2 and Tigris all speak the S3 API, but they sell different things: Wasabi and B2 a low flat price per TB, Tigris data placed near whoever reads it. List prices, checked on 5 October 2026.

rows.label: Egress to the internet
values: Free while monthly egress stays at or below the data stored
Free up to 3× the average data stored, then $0.01 per GB; free through partner CDNs
$0.09 per GB for the first 10 TB, after 100 GB free

rows.label: Request fees
values: Free, except Class D calls: $0.004 per 10,000 after 2,500 a day
$4.50 per million writes, $0.36 per million reads

rows.label: Minimum storage duration
values: None (30 days Infrequent Access, 90 days Archive)
None (30 to 180 days in colder classes)

rows.label: Other minimums, free allowance
values: 1 TB billed every month; objects billed as at least 4 KB
5 GB, 10,000 writes and 100,000 reads free each month
No minimum charge; Free Tier credits for new accounts
10 GB-month, 1 million writes and 10 million reads free each month

rows.label: Regions
values: 16; each bucket lives in the region you pick
4; chosen per account at sign-up and fixed
8 behind one endpoint; Global buckets follow their readers
Each bucket lives in the AWS Region you pick

notes: Wasabi’s price is for North America and EMEA; the S3 prices are for US East (N. Virginia).
A minimum storage duration means an object deleted or overwritten sooner is still billed for the full period. On Wasabi it applies to all pay-as-you-go storage, not just a cold tier.

sections.title: Bucket location types
sections.intro: You pick the location type when you create the bucket, with `LocationConstraint`. It decides where copies live and how fresh a read from another region is. All four cost the same.

rows.label: Global (default)
values: One copy, near the writer; copied on demand to regions that read it
Accessible from any surviving region, per Tigris

rows.label: Multi-region
values: Two or more regions in that geography, chosen by Tigris
A regional outage within the geography

rows.label: Dual-region
values: Losing one of the two regions

rows.label: Single-region
values: Across availability zones in one region

notes: Tigris recommends Multi-region for most workloads that need geographic redundancy, and Dual-region only when rules require data in two specific regions.

story: Ovais Tariq, Himank Chaudhary and Yevgeniy ran storage platform teams at Uber for six years, building systems such as Docstore and Herb for thousands of internal developers. They wanted to offer that kind of platform to everyone. Their first product under the Tigris name, in 2022, was an open-source (Apache 2.0) backend for real-time apps, built on FoundationDB so they could skip rebuilding consistency, fault handling and load balancing themselves.

In April 2023 Tariq met Fly.io’s team, whose pitch was running an app in many regions as easily as in one. Tigris turned that idea to storage: objects written in San Jose should be readable from Sydney at local speed, with no setup. On 14 February 2024 it opened a public beta of globally distributed, S3-compatible object storage on Fly.io, free during the beta, and started billing in July 2024.

A seed round led by Andreessen Horowitz followed in March 2024, and a $25 million Series A led by Spark Capital in October 2025, which Tigris said would pay for its own hardware in data centers. Its customers include AI companies such as fal and Krea.

choices.why: A distributed key-value store with strictly serializable transactions gave the team strong consistency, conditional writes and sharding without writing their own consensus and failure handling.
An S3 bucket lives in one region, so distant users are slow unless you add a CDN. Tigris caches and moves objects to the regions that read them instead.
The founders saw egress as a lock-in tax; free transfer lets the same bucket feed compute at any cloud, which matters most for AI training and inference.
Fly.io users ran apps in many regions but often kept their files on a traditional cloud such as S3. A built-in `fly storage create` removed that gap.
